nameStory: The "creeping" part of this plant's name comes from its low-growing, mat-forming habit as it spreads along the ground. Like other St. John's-worts, it's named after St. John the Baptist, as these yellow-flowered plants traditionally bloom around St. John's Day (June 24th). The "wort" is an old English word simply meaning "plant" or "herb."
description: Creeping St. John's-wort is a small, low-growing perennial that hugs the ground and spreads to form mats in wet areas. This diminutive member of the St. John's-wort family rarely grows more than a few inches tall, with small oval leaves and tiny bright yellow flowers. Unlike its taller cousins, this species is specially adapted for life in boggy, waterlogged soils. It's quite rare in New England, making any sighting special for nature explorers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, creeping mats that hug the ground, rarely rising more than 2-4 inches tall. The stems feel somewhat wiry and spread horizontally across wet soil.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright yellow flowers with 5 petals, much smaller than other St. John's-worts. Each flower is only about 1/4 inch across and sits close to the stem.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. They feel smooth and are often less than half an inch long, with a slightly waxy texture.

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Always found in wet, boggy areas where the soil feels spongy underfoot. The ground around it often squelches when you walk on it.

habitat: Creeping St. John's-wort thrives in wet, acidic soils of bogs, marshes, and soggy meadows throughout New England. You'll find it in areas where water stands for much of the year, often alongside sphagnum moss, sedges, and other bog-loving plants. It prefers full sun to partial shade in these consistently moist to waterlogged conditions.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small, fresh green shoots spreading low across wet ground. The plant begins to fill out its mat-like form as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Blooming occurs with tiny yellow flowers appearing close to the stems. This is the best time for identification when both flowers and full foliage are present.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and small seed capsules develop. The foliage may take on slightly reddish tones before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only roots and possibly some persistent low stems in milder areas.

funFact: This tiny plant is like the "bonsai" of the St. John's-wort family – it has all the classic family features (yellow flowers, opposite leaves, oil glands) but packages them into a ground-hugging form that's perfectly adapted to survive in waterlogged soils where larger plants would literally drown!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small St. John's-worts, but its creeping, mat-forming habit and preference for very wet soils sets it apart. Remember: if it's not in a boggy area and doesn't hug the ground, it's probably a different species.
contextualKnowledge: This species is quite rare in New England with only 11 documented observations, so finding one is truly special. Many St. John's-worts have been used medicinally, but this tiny species was likely too small and uncommon to have much traditional use.
compareHints: Unlike the tall, upright Common St. John's-wort or the bushy shrubby St. John's-wort, creeping St. John's-wort stays close to the ground and forms mats. It's much smaller than Virginia marsh St. John's-wort, which also likes wet areas but grows more upright. The creeping habit combined with the bog habitat makes this species unique among New England's St. John's-worts.
